## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of bitwise rotation, a common low-level primitive in systems and cryptography. 

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation vs shift
- Normalizing k with k & 31
- Safe shifts using (32 - kk) & 31 to avoid 32-bit shifts

## Code Example

```c
uint32_t rotl32(uint32_t n, uint32_t k) {
  uint32_t kk = k & 31;
  return (n << kk) | (n >> ((32 - kk) & 31));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt for 64-bit inputs?
- What are potential compiler/target differences in shifts?

## Why This Is Asked

This question tests precise bit-level reasoning and avoids expensive operations in tight loops, useful in storage engines and query optimizers.

- Single-set-bit test: (n & (n-1)) == 0

## Code Example

function isSingleEvenBitSet(n) {
  return n !== 0 && (n & (n - 1)) === 0 && (n & 0x55555555) !== 0;
}

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests understanding of 128-bit rotation, edge-case handling without branches, and safe shift magnitudes using masking.

## Key Concepts

- Bitwise rotate with shifts
- Modulo-like normalization using masks
- Safe 128-bit shifts without UB

## Code Example

```cpp
uint128 ror128(uint128 x, unsigned int k) {
  k &= 127;
  return (x >> k) | (x << ((128 - k) & 127));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you test this with random k values and ensure no UB?
- How would you adapt for left-rotation and mixed-width types?
